title: The many faces of Ọrun
description: From Yoruba transcription to Unicode: why Ọrun is more than a domain name.
author: PuniCodex Team
body:
# The many faces of Ọrun

No important name has only one face. **Ọrun** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and its roots, the Yoruba transcription original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *orun* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Ọrun
- **ASCII form:** orun
- **Meaning:** ""Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world"
- **Domain of influence:** Sky, Heaven, Destiny
- **Pantheon:** Yoruba
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Live domain:** ọrun.com

## Overview

**Ọrun** (*orun*) — Sky, Heaven, Destiny · "Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world — belongs to the Yoruba tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sky, Heaven, Destiny". The name means ""Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world".

Ọrun is the Yoruba name of heaven itself: the sky-realm where Olódùmarè and the orisha dwell, from which every soul descends to earth (ayé) — and to which every destiny (orí) is assigned before birth. It is not a god but the address of the gods.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Ọrun** and serves its temple at [ọrun.com](https://xn--run-slz.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *orun* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Ọrun** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means ""Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world".

The ASCII form *orun* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Ọrun** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **o** → **Ọ** — Open-mid o with underdot
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same

The project holds the domain **ọrun.com** (xn--run-slz.com) as the canonical home of this name.

## The Original Script

No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual yoruba names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.

The form **Ọrun** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ɔ̀.rún/** — Standard Yoruba.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: aw-ROON — open o (dot-below), low-high melody.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Yoruba** — Ọ̀run
- **Owner of heaven** — Olóòrun
- **Owned form** — Ọrun

Ọrun is Yoruba for "heaven": the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form — the full tone marks (Ọ̀run, low-high) cannot be registered as a domain, so the temple preserves the tone in text while the address bar carries what the DNS allows. The dot-below is the open-mid vowel — the open aw of law — distinct from the close o; the tone is low-high, falling then rising.

## Mythology

Ọrun's myths are the architecture of Yoruba cosmology: how heaven was made, and how souls travel its road to earth.

### The Chain to Earth (The Descent)

In the beginning there was only Ọrun above and the waters below. Olódùmarè sent Odùduwà down with a chain, a rooster, and a handful of earth: the rooster scattered the soil on the water, and the land of Ilé-Ifẹ̀ spread — earth founded beneath heaven, the two realms joined by the road of the orisha. Every Yoruba city thereafter is a point on that first chain's route.

### The Choosing of Orí (The Choice)

Before birth, each soul kneels in Ọrun before Olódùmarè and receives its orí — its inner head, its portion of destiny. The Ifá corpus teaches that the choice, once made, is erased from memory but not from life: every fortune and misfortune on earth is the heaven-chosen head working out its own plot. To pray for a good orí is to negotiate with one's own prenatal self.

### Souls on the Road (The Traffic)

The Yoruba cosmos runs on commuting: the orisha descend to possess their priests, the ancestors visit in dreams and Egúngún masquerades, and the dead return as children ("abíkú" are souls who commute too often). Ọrun is not distant but adjacent — the sky-realm whose door opens in every shrine, every trance, and every correctly cast palm-nut of Ifá.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Ọrun concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The white cloth** — Heaven's color — purity and the unblemished sky
- **The palm nuts** — Ifá's instruments — heaven's messages read on earth
- **The head** — Orí, the chosen destiny — heaven carried inside the skull

## Archaeology & Evidence

Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the city Odùduwà founded on the scattered earth, keeps the creation-site shrines: the Oke Itase hill and the palace of the Ọọni, whose crown descends from heaven's own. The bronze heads of Ifẹ̀ (12th–15th c.), among Africa's supreme artworks, are the faces of heaven's first citizens. The Ifá corpus — the great oral archive — is preserved by the babaláwo lineages of Yorubaland and the diaspora.

## Realm & Domain

Ọrun is the Yoruba name of heaven itself: the sky-realm where Olódùmarè and the orisha dwell, from which every soul descends to earth (ayé) — and to which every destiny (orí) is assigned before birth. It is not a god but the address of the gods.

### Ọrun and Ayé

Heaven and earth: the two halves of reality, with the soul commuting between them.

### Orí

The inner head — the personal destiny each soul chooses (or receives) in Ọrun before birth.

### Olódùmarè

The Owner of Heaven — the supreme being whose realm Ọrun is.

### The Descent

Every birth is an emigration from heaven; every death, the return journey.

### Orí

The inner head — the personal destiny each soul chooses (or receives) in Ọrun before birth.

## Across Cultures

The Ọrun-ayé structure traveled with the diaspora: Candomblé's Oxalá-realm, Santería's heaven of Olófin, and Haiti's lwa-cosmology all keep the two-world map. Christian heaven merged with Ọrun in the New World without ever absorbing it: the Yoruba sky remains a realm of traffic and traffic-officers (the orisha), not of distant thrones — heaven as the next city over, not the next world.

Within the Yoruba tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aganju|Aganjú]], [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[eshu|Ẹṣu]], [[oba|Ọba]], [[obatala|Ọbatálá]], and [[ogun|Ògún]].

## Cultural Legacy

The word lives in a thousand names: Ọrunmila (heaven-knows-salvation), Ọlọrun (owner-of-heaven), Ọrúnmìlà, Ọba-Ọrun. Ifá divination — UNESCO-listed — is its daily news service, and the Egúngún festivals keep the ancestors' visits on the calendar. Every Yoruba funeral says the same thing in ten thousand voices: "the journey to Ọrun is well-traveled" — heaven as home, not as hope.

## A Meditation

Ọrun is the heaven that answers letters. It is not a place you hope to reach but the place you came from — with your destiny already in your pocket, unread. It asks the Yoruba question, which is also everyone's: the head you chose is the life you are living — so what, this morning, will you do with the heaven you brought with you?

And the traffic never stops: the babaláwo casts the nuts at dawn, the Egúngún dance at noon, a child is named for heaven by evening. Ọrun is the least distant heaven ever conceived — next door, upstairs, on the phone. The question is never whether it answers; it is whether we are still calling.

The Ifá verses insist the choosing of orí is both gift and contract: heaven offers, the soul accepts, memory is wiped, and life is the slow reading of the agreement. It is the most humane theory of destiny ever written — you signed it yourself, so stop complaining and start reading. The babaláwo is only the notary.

Every naming ceremony in Yorubaland quietly re-ratifies the architecture: a child arrives from Ọrun with a head already chosen, and the parents spend the child's lifetime reading it. The babaláwo's nuts, the Egúngún's visits, the funeral's road-home — one system, no gaps. Heaven is not the distant answer here; it is the standing arrangement.

And the names go on arriving: Ọlọ́run for the owner, Ọ̀rúnmìlà for the knowing, Ọba-Ọrun for the kingly — heaven filed into a thousand birth certificates, each child a new piece of the sky on earth. The Yoruba answer to 'where is heaven?' was never a direction. It was a custody arrangement, and the paperwork is the people.

So the traffic continues, both ways, always: the sky is not empty, it is staffed — and the commute is the oldest institution in Yorubaland.

Every dawn the road opens again: the sun climbs from the same heaven, and the first prayer goes up by the same old chain, intact.

The rooster that scattered the first earth still crows in the Ifẹ̀ dawn — creation, the tradition says, is a daily event, and heaven signs for every delivery.

## The Unicode Restoration

Ọrun is classified as **Tier 1**: the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses. The ASCII fallback *orun* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 4 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 1: 1 further adjustment (Ọ). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## Character by Character

The journey from *orun* to **Ọrun**, one character at a time:

- **o** → **Ọ** — Open-mid o with underdot
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **ọrun.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--run-slz.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Ọrun; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Yoruba transcription can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does Ọrun mean?** The traditional gloss is ""Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world."

**Which tradition does Ọrun belong to?** Ọrun is catalogued in the Yoruba pantheon of the PuniCodex lexicon.

**Why is Ọrun classified as Tier 1?** Because the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses — and the marks in the restored spelling preserve exactly that evidence.

**Is Ọrun a working domain?** Yes — ọrun.com resolves today and routes to this temple.

**What is the punycode for ọrun.com?** The DNS encoding is xn--run-slz.com; browsers perform the translation automatically, so visitors only ever see the restored name.

**Can I use Ọrun in a normal browser?** Yes. The DNS resolves the punycode form automatically, and the type tool on this site converts orun to Ọrun for copying and pasting.

**Where does the scholarly information come from?** The entry is built from lexica, inscriptional evidence, and reviewed scholarly sources listed in the Scholarly Edition. Every claim is traceable to a canonical source.

You do not need a special keyboard to use this restoration. The [PuniCodex Type Tool](/type/) converts the ASCII form *orun* into **Ọrun** as you type, and the browser extension offers the same conversion inside any text field. Copy the restored form, paste it into the address bar, and the DNS does the rest.

## Why This Restoration Matters

Myth, script, sound, cult, legacy, domain: the faces of Ọrun add up to a single argument — that a name is a record, and records deserve fidelity. The PuniCodex restoration keeps that record in working order: the temple presents it, the Scholarly Edition footnotes it, the lexicon catalogs it, and the domain makes it addressable. *orun* will always exist as a fallback. But fallback is not identity. **Ọrun** is the name; everything else is a convenience.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Ọrun**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *orun* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 4 characters, 3 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **o** becomes **Ọ** — Open-mid o with underdot.

The **r** stays as it is — Same.

The **u** stays as it is — Same.

The **n** stays as it is — Same.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.

## Ọrun in Its Tradition

**Ọrun** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Yoruba tradition, where it is counted among 21 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Sky, Heaven, Destiny — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Ọrun**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Ọrun** is one such vote.
